claims.text: Promoting a uniform atomic distribution during controlled synthesis enhances the catalytic performance of noble metal–based high-entropy alloy nanoparticles.
Varying stoichiometry under controlled synthesis conditions promotes atomic-level homogeneity.
The prescribed thermal, pressure, and precursor-concentration settings favor single-phase formation.
The prescribed synthesis settings minimize phase segregation.
Controlled alloying produces a uniform atomic distribution.
Controlled alloying produces an optimized electronic structure.
Uniform atomic mixing enhances the distribution of catalytic active sites.
Uniform atomic mixing modulates adsorption energies.
Enhanced active-site distribution and modulation of adsorption energies improve reaction kinetics.
Improved reaction kinetics increase overall catalytic activity.
Stoichiometrically optimized and homogenized nanoparticles will have a higher turnover frequency than uncontrolled, compositionally inhomogeneous baseline materials.
Stoichiometrically optimized and homogenized nanoparticles will have greater catalytic stability than uncontrolled, compositionally inhomogeneous baseline materials.
Rapid quenching can serve as an example of synthesis without stoichiometric optimization or homogenization.
Non-optimized equal elemental ratios lead to compositional inhomogeneity.
The proposed relationship is expected to apply to noble metal–based high-entropy alloys capable of forming stable, single-phase solid solutions under the prescribed conditions.
The proposed relationship may not apply to alloy systems with extreme atomic mismatches.
The proposed relationship may not apply under processing regimes that induce phase segregation.
Lattice strain may contribute to catalytic performance independently of atomic uniformity.
Prolonged annealing promotes atomic uniformity relative to rapid quenching.

contradictions.description: The conditions require identical thermal settings, but the proposed comparison uses prolonged annealing for one set and rapid quenching for the control, so thermal history is not held constant.

The stated intervention is stoichiometric variation, whereas the experiment simultaneously changes annealing or quenching history; this confounds the proposed stoichiometry effect with thermal processing.
